notes.title: Number Representation
notes.description: Bits, bases, and the five integer encodings — plus overflow, extension, shifts, and byte order.

notes.title: C
notes.description: Pointers, arrays, strings, structs, the memory layout, malloc/free, and generics.

notes.title: Floating Point
notes.description: IEEE 754 fields, normalized vs. denormalized values, special values, and spacing.

notes.title: RISC-V Assembly
notes.description: Registers, arithmetic, loads and stores, branches, and the calling convention.

notes.title: Instruction Formats
notes.description: R, I, S, B, U, and J encodings, immediates, and PC-relative addressing.

notes.title: CALL
notes.description: Compiler, assembler, linker, loader — who does what, and when symbols get resolved.

notes.title: Digital Logic & SDS
notes.description: Boolean algebra, gates, registers and timing, FSMs, and the adder/ALU blocks.

notes.title: Single-Cycle Datapath
notes.description: The five phases, every control signal, and how to add a new instruction.

notes.title: Pipelining & Hazards
notes.description: The 5-stage pipeline, performance, and structural, data, and control hazards.

notes.title: Caches
notes.description: Locality, tag/index/offset, associativity, replacement, miss types, and AMAT.

notes.title: Parallelism
notes.description: Amdahl's Law, SIMD intrinsics, OpenMP threads, data races, and cache coherence.

notes.title: Virtual Memory
notes.description: Pages, page tables, address translation, the TLB, and the full memory hierarchy.

notes.title: L1 Direct Proofs
notes.description: The lecture introduced CS70 through axiomatic truth, formal language, discrete mathematics, and a specifications-based grading system. It developed direct proofs about even and odd integers, previewed proof by contradiction and propositional logic, and used false algebraic arguments to show why convincing-looking work still requires careful justification.

notes.title: L2 Propositional Logic and Proof Techniques
notes.description: The lecture introduced propositions, predicates, quantifiers, logical connectives, truth tables, contrapositives, and De Morgan's laws. It used the card-selection problem and the parity of an integer product to show how formal logic clarifies natural-language statements and supports proof by example, counterexample, and contrapositive.
notes.file: cs70/Lecture Notes/L2 Propositional Logic and Proof Techniques.md

notes.title: L3 Proof Techniques
notes.description: The lecture introduced biconditional proofs and reviewed direct and contrapositive proof techniques through parity and divisibility examples. It then developed proof by contradiction using a linear combination and began the classical argument that square root of 2 is irrational, which remained incomplete in the recorded portion.

notes.title: L4 Induction
notes.description: The lecture reviewed proof by cases and introduced mathematical induction through sums of odd numbers, the domino analogy, and the connection to recursion. It emphasized the necessity of a base case, developed the inductive hypothesis and inductive step, and began motivating strong induction through prime factorizations.

notes.title: L5 Modular Arithmetic
notes.description: The lecture develops modular arithmetic as arithmetic on a circle, formalizes congruence through remainders and divisibility, and explains congruence classes and substitution in modular calculations. It applies these ideas to divisibility tests, efficient modular exponentiation by repeated squaring, and additive and multiplicative inverses.

notes.title: L6 Euclid, FLT, CRT
notes.description: The lecture developed greatest common divisors, relative primality, Bézout's identity, and the Euclidean and extended Euclidean algorithms, with geometric and algebraic walkthroughs. It then introduced modular inverses, a switch-based construction for simultaneous congruences, the Chinese remainder theorem, and Fermat's little theorem.

notes.title: L7 RSA
notes.description: The lecture reviewed the Chinese remainder theorem, Fermat's little theorem, and exponent reduction in modular arithmetic before applying them to RSA. It developed public-key encryption, derived the RSA decryption exponent and correctness argument, discussed computational hardness, and concluded with surprising digit patterns under elementary arithmetic.

notes.title: L8 Polynomials
notes.description: The lecture introduced polynomials, their coefficients and degrees, and two structural properties concerning roots and interpolation. It developed Lagrange interpolation, explained polynomials over finite fields, and applied interpolation to threshold secret sharing.

notes.title: L9 Secret Sharing & Error-Correcting Codes
notes.description: The lecture reviewed Shamir secret sharing and showed how polynomial shares can assign different recovery power to contributors and moderators. It then developed Reed-Solomon codes for erasure and general errors, proved the required redundancy bounds used in the lecture, and derived the Berlekamp-Welch decoder from an error-locator polynomial and a system of linear equations.
notes.file: cs70/Lecture Notes/L9 Secret Sharing & Error-Correcting Codes.md

notes.title: L10 Graphs I
notes.description: The lecture introduced graphs as abstractions of objects and their connections, then defined neighborhoods, degree, paths, cycles, walks, tours, connectivity, and Eulerian tours. Using the Seven Bridges of Konigsberg, it motivated Euler's theorem and sketched both the parity argument and a recursive algorithm for constructing an Eulerian tour.

notes.title: L10 Graphs II
notes.description: The lecture develops the handshake lemma and uses it to count edges in complete graphs and hypercubes. It then studies equivalent descriptions of trees, proves that every nontrivial tree has a leaf, uses graph induction to count tree edges, and introduces bipartite and planar graphs.

notes.title: L12 Stable Matching
notes.description: The lecture concluded the graph unit with the handshake lemma, complete graphs, trees, hypercubes, bipartite graphs, and planar graphs. It developed a constructive leaf argument, a graph-induction proof for the edge count of a tree, and counting walkthroughs for hypercubes and planar graphs.

notes.title: L13 Countability
notes.description: The lecture introduced the proposer-rejector stable matching algorithm, defined rogue pairs and stable matchings, and proved that the algorithm halts, outputs a matching, and produces a stable matching. It also developed the improvement lemma and explained proposer-optimal and rejector-pessimal outcomes, contrasting the two-group setting with a roommate example that has no stable matching.

notes.title: L14 Computability
notes.description: The foundations of computability through self-reference, Hilbert's program, and Gödel's incompleteness theorem. Includes the diagonalization proof that the halting problem is undecidable and a reduction showing that deciding halting on the fixed input zero is equally hard.

notes.title: L15 Counting
notes.description: The lecture concluded the discrete mathematics portion of the course with guidance about synthesis questions, then introduced four counting problems organized by whether order matters and replacement is allowed. It derived permutations, combinations, counting with replacement, a binary-string bijection for unordered sampling with replacement, and a counting proof of the binomial theorem.

notes.title: L16 Intro to Discrete Probability
notes.description: The lecture formalized random experiments, sample spaces, probability functions, and events while distinguishing uniform from nonuniform probability spaces. It applied counting methods to dice, coin flips, poker hands, balls and bins, and the birthday paradox, with particular emphasis on choosing an ordered model to obtain a uniform probability space.
notes.file: cs70/Lecture Notes/L16 Intro to Discrete Probability.md

notes.title: L17 Conditional Probability
notes.description: The lecture develops conditional probability for outcomes and events, derives the intersection formula, and applies it to dice, cards, shopping centers, and the Monty Hall problem. It then introduces prior and posterior probabilities, the total probability rule, and Bayes' rule through flu-testing and restaurant-selection walkthroughs.

notes.title: L18 Combinations of Events
notes.description: The lecture developed the principle of inclusion-exclusion from set counting and proved it by tracking how often each element is counted. It then introduced independence, mutual independence, and the product rule before applying inclusion-exclusion, complements, and truncation bounds to probabilities of unions.

notes.title: L19 Random Variables and Expectation
notes.description: The lecture defined random variables as functions from sample outcomes to real numbers, then developed events, distributions, probability mass functions, and expectation through coin, dice, and homework-permutation examples. It also introduced Bernoulli, binomial, uniform, and geometric random variables, including the geometric distribution's tail probabilities and memoryless property.
notes.file: cs70/Lecture Notes/L19 Random Variables and Expectation.md

notes.title: L20 Random Variables II, Linearity of Expectation
notes.description: The lecture introduced Poisson random variables, derived their probability mass function as a large-trial limit of binomial random variables, and showed how independent Poisson variables combine. It then developed joint and marginal distributions, independence and conditioning for random variables, IID variables, and linearity of expectation with dice and randomized homework examples.
notes.file: cs70/Lecture Notes/L20 Random Variables II, Linearity of Expectation.md

notes.title: CS 70 HW 02 — Induction, Modular Arithmetic, Check Digits, and Number Theory
notes.description: Homework on mathematical induction, modular arithmetic, congruence foundations, ISBN check digits, Fibonacci GCDs, and number-theoretic stretch problems.

notes.title: CS 70 HW 04 — Secret Sharing, Polynomials, Interpolation, and Error Correction
notes.description: Homework on secret-sharing scheme design, polynomial degree properties, Lagrange interpolation over GF(7), Reed-Solomon error-locator polynomials, equivalent polynomials modulo a prime, and adversarial packet corruption, plus two stretch problems on Reed-Solomon tightness and malicious secret-sharing shares.

notes.title: CS 70 HW 05 — Graphs, Trees, Eulerian Tours, Connectivity, and Planarity
notes.description: Homework on graph basics, planar graph formulas, tree properties, Eulerian tours, connectivity, hypercube tours, and graph complements, plus a graph-coloring stretch problem and an optional mountain-range challenge.

notes.title: CS 70 HW 07 Solutions — Countability and Computability
notes.description: Official HW 07 solutions, each placed directly under its question: injections and surjections, Cantor-Bernstein, the Halting Problem by reduction and by diagonalization, classifying sets as finite, countable, or uncountable, and two unprogrammable programs.

notes.title: CS 70 HW 08 Solutions — Counting and Probability Basics
notes.description: Official HW 08 solutions, each placed directly under its question: counting with and without order and replacement, sample spaces and events, PINs, anagrams, card hands, stars and bars, Minesweeper, parking lots, and the necklace-counting stretch problem.

notes.title: CS 70 HW 09 Solutions — Conditional Probability and Combinations of Events
notes.description: Official HW 09 solutions, each placed directly under its question: conditional probability, Bayes' Rule, total probability, inclusion-exclusion, independence of complements, balls and bins with the union bound, and the dining-hall and socks stretch problems.

notes.title: CS 70 HW 10 Solutions — Random Variables and Linearity of Expectation
notes.description: Official HW 10 solutions, each placed directly under its question: distributions, expectation, indicators and linearity, joint distributions and independence, Bernoulli, Binomial, Geometric, and Poisson models, and the swaps-and-cycles and office-hour-queue stretch problems.

notes.description: Proof by contraposition, proof by contradiction, proof by cases, common proof-writing errors, and general advice for constructing rigorous proofs.

notes.title: N4 Mathematical Induction
notes.description: Proof by mathematical induction, including base cases and inductive steps, strengthening the induction hypothesis, simple versus strong induction, and the connection between induction and recursively defined algorithms.

notes.title: N5 Modular Arithmetic
notes.description: Modular arithmetic and residue classes, computing sums, differences, and products modulo m, fast modular exponentiation by repeated squaring, and the existence and uniqueness of multiplicative inverses.

notes.title: N6 Euclid's Algorithm, Unique Factorization, and Modular Arithmetic
notes.description: Euclid's algorithm and its extension for computing gcds and multiplicative inverses, the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, the Chinese Remainder Theorem, and Fermat's Little Theorem.

notes.title: N7 Public Key Cryptography
notes.description: The RSA public-key cryptosystem: encryption and decryption via modular exponentiation, the proof of RSA's correctness using Fermat's Little Theorem and the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the security assumption underlying RSA, and practical implementation considerations.

notes.title: N8 Polynomials, Finite Fields, and Secret Sharing
notes.description: Properties of polynomials (bounds on roots, uniqueness of interpolating polynomials), Lagrange interpolation, polynomial division, finite fields, counting polynomials by coefficient and value representation, and a secret-sharing scheme built from polynomial interpolation over a finite field.
notes.file: cs70/Course Notes/N8 Polynomials, Finite Fields, and Secret Sharing.md

notes.title: N9 Error-Correcting Codes
notes.description: Reed-Solomon-style error-correcting codes built from polynomials over finite fields: recovering a message from erasure errors via Lagrange interpolation, a linear-algebra method for polynomial interpolation, and the Berlekamp-Welch algorithm for locating and correcting general (corruption) errors.

notes.title: CS 70 Note 10 — Graph Theory, Eulerian Tours, Trees, Planarity, and Hypercubes
notes.description: Introduces graphs, paths, connectivity, Eulerian tours, complete graphs, and trees. Develops Euler's formula and non-planarity criteria, then studies hypercube connectivity and de Bruijn sequences.

notes.title: CS 70 Note 11 — Stable Matching and the Propose-and-Reject Algorithm
notes.description: Develops the Propose-and-Reject algorithm for stable matching, proves termination and stability using the Improvement Lemma, and introduces the well-ordering principle. Proves that the resulting matching is employer optimal and candidate pessimal.

notes.title: CS 70 Note 12 — Countability, Diagonalization, and Orders of Infinity
notes.description: Uses bijections and injections to compare infinite sets and establish the countability of integers, rationals, finite strings, and polynomials. Develops Cantor's diagonalization, the uncountability of the Cantor set, and the larger cardinality of power sets.

notes.title: CS 70 Note 13 — Self-Reference and Computability
notes.description: Connects self-reference, quines, and the recursion theorem to the limits of computation. Proves the uncomputability of the Halting Problem, reduces it to the Easy Halting Problem, and sketches Gödel's Incompleteness Theorem through self-reference and proof enumeration.

notes.title: CS 70 Note 15 — Counting
notes.description: Develops the rules of counting for sequences and sets, with and without replacement and with or without regard to order. Covers the zeroth, first, and second rules of counting, stars-and-bars for multisets, the Binomial Theorem, and bonus material on combinatorial identities and derangements.

notes.title: CS 70 Note 16 — Introduction to Discrete Probability
notes.description: Introduces random experiments, sample spaces, probability spaces, and events, and shows how probabilities of events reduce to counting in uniform spaces. Worked examples cover coin tosses, dice, card shuffling, poker hands, balls and bins, and the birthday paradox.
notes.file: cs70/Course Notes/N16 Introduction to Discrete Probability.md

notes.title: CS 70 Note 17 — Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule
notes.description: Defines conditional probability and applies it to card dealing, the Monty Hall problem, and Bayesian inference. Derives Bayes' Rule and the Total Probability Rule, with worked examples and the generalization to partitions of the sample space.
notes.file: cs70/Course Notes/N17 Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule.md

notes.title: CS 70 Note 18 — Inclusion-Exclusion and Combinations of Events
notes.description: Proves the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion and applies it to derangements, then develops independence, the Product Rule, and inclusion-exclusion for probabilities of unions, ending with the union bound. Examples include coin tosses, Monty Hall, poker hands, and a Las Vegas dice game.
notes.file: cs70/Course Notes/N18 Inclusion-Exclusion and Combinations of Events.md

notes.title: CS 70 Note 19 — Random Variables, Distribution and Expectation
notes.description: Defines random variables, their distributions, and expectation, with the tail sum formula. Covers the Bernoulli, binomial, uniform, and geometric distributions, including the memoryless property and the expectation of a geometric random variable.
notes.file: cs70/Course Notes/N19 Random Variables - Distribution and Expectation.md

notes.title: CS 70 Note 20 — Random Variables II, Linearity of Expectation
notes.description: Develops the Poisson distribution and its expectation, proves it is the limit of binomial distributions, and introduces joint distributions, independence of random variables, and sums of independent Poissons. Proves linearity of expectation and applies it to dice, roulette, fixed points, coin tosses, and balls and bins.

notes.title: Data C104 Lecture 1 - Technology, Politics, and Context 08-26
notes.description: The opening Data C104 lecture introduced the course through data-center politics, Langdon Winner's account of political artifacts, and four tools for analyzing human contexts and ethics. The instructors also explained attendance, discussion, reading, assessment, and support arrangements before framing ethical action as dependent on understanding context.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L1 - Technology, Politics, and Context 08-26.md

notes.title: L2 Making the Datafied World 2
notes.description: The lecture introduced the datafied world as an environment in which ubiquitous data, analytics, algorithms, and AI or machine learning systems shape individual and collective life. Using rental-pricing algorithms as a case study, it applied the HCE lenses of power, sociotechnical systems, identity and positionality, and narratives to show how technologies and social relations jointly structure markets, decisions, and possible futures.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L2 Making the Datafied World 2.md

notes.title: L3 Making Data
notes.description: The lecture argued that data is actively made through human labor, choices, standards, classifications, and institutional purposes rather than simply found. Using Bay Area air-quality and refinery-flare data, it examined representation, abstraction, decontextualization, and power, showing how the making of data shapes what can be known and what actions can be taken.

notes.title: L4 Making Personal Data
notes.description: The lecture examined how personal data is made through representation, classification, abstraction, circulation, durability, and relationships among people and institutions. Examples involving university records, punch cards, apartheid-era racial classification, genetic testing, and data-driven harms showed how personal data can speak for people, structure access, and create unequal forms of vulnerability.

notes.title: L5 Making People Out of Data
notes.description: The lecture introduced performativity as a tool for understanding how words, classifications, measurements, and personal data do more than represent reality: they also shape how reality appears and how people act. Through cases including multiple personality disorder, gender, measurement standards, GDP, self-tracking, and personality tests, it argued that data participates in making identities, institutions, social relations, and forms of selfhood.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L5 Making People Out of Data.md

notes.title: L6 Making Robust Knowledge
notes.description: The lecture examined how scientific knowledge can be both made by human beings and robust under scrutiny. It compared scientific method, logical positivism, falsification, underdetermination, and Thomas Kuhn's account of paradigms to argue that robustness arises through the practices and social organization of scientific communities.

notes.title: L7 Science in Society
notes.description: The lecture examines expertise, public trust, and socially robust scientific knowledge by placing science within its broader institutional and political relationships. Cases involving climate change, Cumbrian sheep farming after Chernobyl, earthquake risk in Italy, and Pasteur illustrate how inclusion, communication, funding, uncertainty, and public engagement shape scientific authority.

notes.title: L8 Population and States
notes.description: The lecture traced the intertwined emergence of populations, modern states, and statistics from early modern European state-building through nineteenth-century social physics. It examined political arithmetic, German Statistik, administrative standardization, censuses, and the normal distribution as practices that made people legible, governable, and comparable.

notes.title: L9 Eugenics and Statistics
notes.description: The lecture traced how Francis Galton’s study of heredity and social hierarchy contributed to linear regression, correlation, and eugenics, then connected this history to the work of Karl Pearson and Ronald Fisher. It examined eugenics as a form of biopower, followed its institutional expression in Britain, the United States, California, and Stanford, and argued that understanding this history can make contemporary data science more reflective about its assumptions, examples, and institutional roles.

notes.title: L10 Taking the Global View
notes.description: The lecture traced how states and postwar international institutions developed data infrastructures for viewing and governing populations, economies, and territories from above. It used Gapminder's fertility and child-mortality visualization to examine how global statistics embed assumptions about development, representation, reproductive life, and who has the power to define problems and desirable futures.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L10 Taking the Global View.md

notes.title: L12 Privacy in the World
notes.description: The lecture argued that a 1970s model of privacy based on individual control, consent, and personally identifiable information is inadequate for a datafied world. Through cases involving Indigenous blood samples, crisis-support conversations, university data, and airport body scanners, it introduced contextual integrity and examined privacy in relation to power, dignity, identity, collective interests, and data minimization.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L12 Privacy in the World.md

notes.title: L15 Making Decisions
notes.description: The lecture historicized decision making as a modern model of agency and rationality rather than a timeless description of human action. It connected behaviorism, cybernetics, game theory, rational choice, bounded rationality, behavioral economics, and choice architecture to institutional efforts to model, predict, and shape behavior.

notes.title: L16 Fairness Automated Decision-Making I
notes.description: The lecture introduced algorithmic fairness through automated decision-making in criminal justice, focusing on competing interpretations of error rates in the Compass risk-assessment case. It argued that fairness cannot be reduced to technical accuracy because data, classifications, institutional practices, social identities, and the consequences of errors are intertwined.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L16 Fairness Automated Decision-Making I.md

notes.title: L17 Automated Decision Making II - Prediction
notes.description: The lecture examined predictive automated decision making as a political and institutional practice whose fairness cannot be reduced to statistical accuracy or the absence of bias. Through cases involving exam grades, criminal justice, child welfare, insurance, and credit, it connected prediction to due process, representation, agency, surveillance, bureaucracy, risk, and the production of social order.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L17 Automated Decision Making II - Prediction.md

notes.title: L18 Automated Decision Making III - Risk
notes.description: The lecture traces how risk assessment, insurance, actuarial fairness, and automated decision-making developed together as ways of organizing social life. It contrasts solidaristic pooling with individualized risk pricing, connects the latter to neoliberal governance, and examines how predictive systems sort, discipline, personalize, and modulate behavior.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L18 Automated Decision Making III - Risk.md

notes.title: L19 Data Futures
notes.description: The lecture examined narratives and futuring as ways of imagining datafied worlds and shaping action in the present. Through cases including the sewing machine, electronic health records, smart cities, dystopian fiction, and AI imagery, it argued that technological futures are selective, performative, sociotechnical, and shaped by positionality.

notes.title: L20 AI Futures
notes.description: The lecture examined AI futures as narratives that organize technological history, define the human, and make particular outcomes appear desirable, catastrophic, or inevitable. Through 2001: A Space Odyssey, existential risk, longtermism, transhumanism, immortality, and robot labor, it connected AI speculation to power, political economy, class, gender, race, and alternative forms of storytelling.

notes.title: L21 Automation and Labor
notes.description: analytical notes synthesizing Lecture 21 on Automation and Labor with David F. Noble's study on social choice in machine tool design.

notes.title: L22 Making Silicon Valley I
notes.description: The lecture introduced Silicon Valley as a geography, a narrative about technological change, a mechanism for imagining futures, and a machine for producing wealth and social order. It developed the standard history through layers of agriculture, wireless and aviation, Stanford's institutional growth, wartime industry, and semiconductor production while examining the networks, state power, labor, and omissions beneath that history.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L22 Making Silicon Valley I.md

notes.title: L23 Making Silicon Valley II
notes.description: The lecture examined how narratives, venture capital, startup culture, and software shaped Silicon Valley alongside technical innovation. It connected the marketing of personal computers and myths of founders working from garages to financial models built around risk, rapid scaling, market dominance, and recurring cycles of investment.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L23 Making Silicon Valley II.md

notes.title: L24 Making Silicon Valley III
notes.description: The lecture traces Silicon Valley from the dot-com crash through platform businesses, data extraction, gig labor, cloud computing, and the capital-intensive AI economy. It argues that these developments extend a recurring playbook centered on venture capital, rapid scaling, market dominance, and infrastructure, before examining the renewed convergence of technology firms, state power, and military contracting.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L24 Making Silicon Valley III.md

notes.title: L25 The Tech Workplace Part 1
notes.description: The lecture examined Silicon Valley workplace culture as a historically contingent system of behavioral scripts, hierarchies, rewards, recruitment practices, and narratives about founders and technical work. It used perspectives from workers positioned outside or below the culture's dominant roles to analyze invisible labor, organizational boundaries, homophily, job precarity, and the unequal distribution of workplace opportunities and risks.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L25 The Tech Workplace Part 1.md

notes.title: L27 Environmental Contexts and Consequences of Data
notes.description: The lecture examined the material infrastructure, resource extraction, labor, pollution, and land use underlying computing and data systems. Historical cases from semiconductor manufacturing in Silicon Valley were connected to consumer AI devices and contemporary data centers through the concepts of externalities, invisibilization, and unevenly distributed environmental burdens.
notes.file: datac104/Lecture Notes/L27 Environmental Contexts and Consequences of Data.md

notes.title: Ian Hacking - Making Up People
notes.description: A comprehensive analysis of Ian Hacking's clinical classifications, exploring the concepts of dynamic nominalism, the looping effect, and the ten engines of human classification.

notes.title: Race Classification and Reclassification under Apartheid
notes.description: A detailed analysis of Bowker and Star's Chapter 6, exploring race classification, bureaucratic violence, and the epistemological clash of sorting mechanisms.

notes.title: Notes on Collins and Pinch - Chernobyl and the Cumbrian Sheepfarmers
notes.description: A comprehensive analysis of Chapter 6 from The Golem at Large, detailing the clash between bureaucratic scientific modeling and lay expertise during the 1986 radioactive sheep crisis in Cumbria.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 3/Collins and Pinch - Chernobyl and the Cumbrian Sheepfarmers.md

notes.title: Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
notes.description: A comprehensive analysis of Thomas Kuhn's foundational work, detailing the cycle of normal science, paradigms, crisis, and the sociotechnical and cognitive mechanics of scientific revolutions.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 3/Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions.md

notes.title: Aubrey Clayton's How Eugenics Shaped Statistics
notes.description: A comprehensive analysis of the historical, theoretical, and philosophical entanglement of early mathematical statistics and the eugenics movement.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 4/Aubrey Clayton's How Eugenics Shaped Statistics.md

notes.title: James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State (Chapter 1)
notes.description: A comprehensive analysis of Chapter 1 of James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State, exploring how states employ tunnel vision, legibility, and geometric simplifications to manage forests, measurement, and land tenure.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 4/James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State (Chapter 1).md

notes.title: Why Are Certain Countries Poor - Dismantling Comparative Models of Development
notes.description: A comprehensive analysis of Chapter 8 from Andrew Brooks' work, deconstructing comparative development models (Rostow, HDI) in favor of relational frameworks, with case studies on Mozambique and Sierra Leone's brain drain.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 4/Why Are Certain Countries Poor - Dismantling Comparative Models of Development.md

notes.description: Reading Notes/Week 5

notes.title: Helen Nissenbaum’s Theory of Contextual Integrity
notes.description: A comprehensive analysis of the Contextual Integrity (CI) privacy framework, detailing its five parameters of informational flow, the moral evaluation of novel technologies, and its application to sociotechnical systems.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 5/Helen Nissenbaum’s Theory of Contextual Integrity.md

notes.title: The Right to Oblivion - Privacy and the Good Life
notes.description: A comprehensive philosophical analysis of Lowry Pressly's introduction to The Right to Oblivion, tracing the boundary lines between privacy, secrecy, hiding, and the vital role of oblivion in human flourishing.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 5/The Right to Oblivion - Privacy and the Good Life.md

notes.title: Michel Foucault's Discipline and Punish (Panopticism)
notes.description: A comprehensive analysis of Foucault's seminal text on panopticism, tracing the historical transition from plague-era containment to the modern disciplinary mechanics of Bentham's Panopticon.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 6/Michel Foucault's Discipline and Punish (Panopticism).md

notes.title: Theodore Porter's Objectivity and Authority - How French Engineers Reduced Public Utility to Numbers
notes.description: A comprehensive analysis of Theodore Porter's 1991 paper, exploring the social and political origins of scientific objectivity, the rise of quantification in democratic public life, and the mathematical economics of the elite French engineering corps.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 6/Theodore Porter's Objectivity and Authority - How French Engineers Reduced Public Utility to Numbers.md

notes.title: Fourcade and Healy – Classification Situations
notes.description: Comprehensive analytical notes on Chapter 3 ("Classification Situations") of Marion Fourcade and Kieran Healy's The Ordinal Society, covering digital data doubles, panoptic sorting, nominal vs. ordinal judgment, algorithmic failure modes, and the dimensions of eigencapital.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 7/Fourcade and Healy – Classification Situations.md

notes.title: Virginia Eubanks' Automating Inequality (Chapter 4)
notes.description: A comprehensive pedagogical analysis of Chapter 4 of Automating Inequality, detailing the mechanical operations, structural class biases, and ethical feedback loops of the Allegheny Family Screening Tool (AFST).

notes.title: David F. Noble - Social Choice in Machine Design The Case of Automatically Controlled Machine Tools
notes.description: Comprehensive analytical notes on David F. Noble's study of automatically controlled machine tools, contrasting numerical control (N/C) and record-playback to demonstrate how managerial control, military funding, and anti-labor ideology shape technological evolution.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 8/David F. Noble - Social Choice in Machine Design The Case of Automatically Controlled Machine Tools.md

notes.title: Hildebrandt Introduction – Dianas OnLife World
notes.description: Analytical notes on Mireille Hildebrandt's introduction to Diana's onlife world, examining technological regulation, democratic law, data-driven agency, and legal protection by design.

notes.title: Marc Andreessen - The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
notes.description: Comprehensive analytical notes on Marc Andreessen's 2023 essay "The Techno-Optimist Manifesto," detailing his arguments for techno-capital accelerationism, market-driven abundance, intelligence and energy feedback loops, and his critique of precautionary stagnationism.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 8/Marc Andreessen - The Techno-Optimist Manifesto.md

notes.title: Ursula K. Le Guin - The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction
notes.description: Comprehensive analytical notes on Ursula K. Le Guin's 1986 essay "The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction," detailing her critique of heroic technological narratives, her redefinition of tools as containers, and her vision of the novel as a vessel for ongoing human life.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 8/Ursula K. Le Guin - The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction.md

notes.title: Kate Crawford - The Atlas of AI (Chapter 2 Labor)
notes.description: Comprehensive analytical notes on Chapter 2 of Kate Crawford's "The Atlas of AI," analyzing algorithmic management, historical lineages of industrial discipline (Bentham, Babbage, Taylor, Ford), Potemkin AI, fauxtomation, ghost work, planetary temporal control, and shop-floor labor struggles at Amazon.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 9/Kate Crawford - The Atlas of AI (Chapter 2 Labor).md

notes.title: Mona Sloane - The Business of AI
notes.description: Comprehensive analytical notes on Chapter 4 of Mona Sloane's "Predicted," examining the political economy of the prediction paradigm, data and material extraction, the social construction of skill and servitude, epistemic clashes over professional discretion, and the gendered hierarchies governing workplace automation.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 9/Mona Sloane - The Business of AI.md

notes.title: Tianyu M Fang - Silicon Valley Goes To War
notes.description: Comprehensive analytical notes on Tianyu M. Fang's essay examining Silicon Valley's structural pivot from consumer-facing digital utopianism to defense technology, the historical revival of Cold War military-industrial ties, and the ethical contradictions of the "Democracy Paradox."
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 9/Tianyu M Fang - Silicon Valley Goes To War.md

notes.title: Tom Nicholas The Emergence of Silicon Valley
notes.description: Comprehensive analytical notes on Chapter 6 of Tom Nicholas's \"VC: An American History,\" examining the tripartite origins of Silicon Valley, the institutional catalysts of academic-industrial clusters, Cold War military procurement, open cultural and legal norms, and the emergence of foundational venture capital investment styles.
notes.file: datac104/Reading Notes/Week 9/Tom Nicholas The Emergence of Silicon Valley.md
